parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

The History of the Pencil

How a chance discovery in an English valley reshaped writing, warfare and industry

The history of the pencil begins, improbably, with a violent thunderstorm. When particularly ferocious weather struck the Lake District in north-west England during the sixteenth century, villagers in Borrowdale found that a large tree had been uprooted. Beneath its exposed roots lay an unfamiliar black substance, slightly shiny and smooth to the touch, which left a dark smear on the hands of anyone who handled it. Why the deposit had remained unnoticed for so long is debatable: some historians attribute it to the remoteness of the valley, while others argue that the local economy simply had no use for such a material until the storm forced it into view. Either way, the consequences of that single event would extend far beyond a quiet farming community.

The first recorded use of the material was strikingly humble. Local farmers used it to mark their sheep, since it adhered stuck to wool and resisted rain. Before long, however, others recognised a more far-reaching possibility, namely that the substance could be used to write on paper. In its untreated state it was extremely soft, and therefore messy to handle, so people enclosed a thin core of it in stiff sheep hides or in lengths of rope. Because chemistry was still in its infancy, the new material was poorly understood. Searching for a name, scholars settled on plumbago, Latin for that which acts or writes like lead. The label was later corrected to graphite once it became clear that the deposit contained no lead at all, yet language proved more durable than chemistry: we still speak of the lead of a pencil, a small linguistic fossil of an error long since disproved.

Graphite owes its strategic importance to a single physical property. With a melting point of roughly 3,500 degrees Celsius, it could withstand temperatures that destroyed most other linings, and this made it invaluable to the British army and navy. The Royal Ordnance, the weaponry division of the armed forces, used graphite to line the moulds in which cannonballs were cast. Because the moulds resisted heat and released the metal cleanly, Britain could produce cannonballs faster and more cheaply than its European rivals, gaining an advantage that was as much economic as military. Recognising this dual value, the government assumed control of the Borrowdale mines during the sixteenth century. Armed guards escorted the graphite all the way to the metal foundries beside the naval shipyards in southern England. The deposit was so valuable that locals, who called it wadd, began stealing it, and in 1752 an Act of Parliament made the theft of graphite punishable by imprisonment, a measure that reveals just how precious the material had become.

If Britain controlled the raw material, it was elsewhere that the pencil took its modern shape. Italian craftsmen are usually credited with inventing the wooden casing: they hollowed out two thin sections of cedar, laid a rod of graphite into one, glued the second over the top, and left the halves to set, producing the familiar object recognisable today. German manufacturers then transformed the craft into an industry by applying early mass-production techniques. The most significant breakthrough, however, came from France. In the late 1700s, Nicolas-Jacques Conté, an officer in Napoleon Bonaparte’s army, devised a method of mixing powdered graphite with clay and firing the mixture in a kiln. The proportions could be adjusted at will: adding more clay produced a harder, sharper and more precise mark, while adding more graphite produced one that was softer, thicker and darker. For the first time, the quality of a pencil could be controlled rather than left to the chance composition of the ore.

Conté’s innovation had a lasting and somewhat unexpected consequence. Because hardness and blackness could now be varied deliberately, manufacturers needed a way to describe the differences, and the result was the grading system still used worldwide. In it, H denotes the hardness of the pencil and B its blackness, with an HB pencil occupying the middle ground as a standard, all-purpose tool; further letters and numbers designate the remaining grades. It is worth noting that this orderly system was not imposed from above but emerged gradually as different makers converged on a shared vocabulary, which helps explain why it took hold so thoroughly and why no rival scheme ever displaced it.

The geography of graphite has shifted considerably since those early days. China now produces most of the world’s pencils, yet the Borrowdale mines remain the only significant source of graphite in its near-pure form anywhere in the world. The highest grade there is now exhausted, although lower grades survive, and England’s pencil industry continues to thrive in the nearby town of Keswick. The pencil itself has proved remarkably resilient, surviving well into the high-tech age, a persistence often illustrated by a popular anecdote. The story claims that the American space programme spent millions developing a pen that could write in zero gravity, while the Russians simply handed their astronauts ordinary pencils. The tale is appealing but false. In reality, astronauts of both nations used pencils on their earliest flights, and a private company later developed the zero-gravity pen that astronauts of every nation now use. The myth endures less because it is accurate than because it flatters a particular view of practical wisdom over expensive ingenuity. Whatever the truth of that contrast, pencils remain in use in every classroom, drawing office and art studio in the world, and there is little to suggest we will soon find anything better than graphite to write with.

parts.name: Passage 2
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Bringing Back the Bittern

How research, not luck, reversed the decline of one of Britain’s most secretive birds

A. The bittern is a heron-like wetland bird whose fortunes in Britain have swung dramatically over little more than a century. Breeding birds had vanished entirely by 1886, yet after re-colonisation in the early 1900s the population climbed to a peak of roughly 70 booming, or singing, males in the 1950s. From there it fell sharply, dropping below 20 by the 1990s. By the late 1980s it was obvious that the species was again in trouble, but conservationists faced an awkward problem: they could see the decline without understanding its causes, and almost no reliable information existed on which to base a recovery. Saving the bird would therefore depend less on goodwill than on first learning how it lived.

B. That task was complicated by the bittern itself. Its mottled plumage and retiring habits keep it hidden deep within reedbeds, so the first challenge was simply to develop a dependable way of monitoring a bird that is rarely seen. The solution lay in sound. During the breeding season the male produces a distinctive booming call, and researchers discovered that the acoustic pattern of each bird is effectively unique. By analysing these patterns they could not only establish how many males were present nationally, but also recognise individuals from one year to the next, which in turn allowed local survival rates to be estimated. A bird that resisted direct observation had, in effect, been persuaded to identify itself.

C. With a counting method in place, attention turned to habitat. The earliest insight came not from new fieldwork but from comparison: sites that had lost their booming males were set against those that had kept them. The contrast was revealing. Bitterns had persisted precisely where the natural drying out of reedbeds, a process known as succession, had been deliberately slowed through management. This finding translated directly into action. Broad recommendations on restoring and maintaining reedbeds were drawn up, and EU LIFE funding enabled work at thirteen sites across the core breeding range. Although the project was led by the RSPB, its success depended on many other organisations, an early sign that recovery would be collaborative rather than the work of a single body.

D. General advice, however, was not the same as precise instruction, and the next phase aimed to replace broad guidance with exact prescriptions. By fitting male bitterns with radio tags at the Minsmere and Leighton Moss reserves, researchers could follow where the birds actually fed. A clear preference emerged for the wetter margins of the reedbed, especially the fringes beside larger pools of open water. The average territory covered around twenty hectares, a figure that gave managers a concrete target for how much reedbed a new or restored site would need. The females told a different but equally important story: since they alone incubate the eggs and raise the young, their needs mattered just as much. Of the eighty-seven nests located, most lay in unbroken vegetation well inside the reedbed, yet always where water remained even in the driest weeks of the season.

E. The effect of applying these prescriptions was striking. At Minsmere, where reedbeds were lowered to halt the drying process, the number of booming males climbed steadily from one to ten. Nationally, the population reached its lowest point of just eleven booming males in 1997 and then, for the first time since the 1950s, began to rise. The recovery was not coincidental; it tracked the management work closely, with the clearest gains appearing exactly where the research-based methods had been applied. For a programme that had begun with almost no usable data, the match between effort and outcome was persuasive evidence that the underlying science was sound.

F. Even so, counting adults could not by itself secure the future, and a later phase examined the diet, survival and movements of the chicks. Tiny radio tags fitted to nestlings traced their fate up to fledging and beyond, and the findings were sobering: many chicks never survived, with starvation the most probable cause. The fish they were fed came overwhelmingly from species that penetrate into the reed edge, which shifted the focus of conservation once again. If the chicks were starving, the reedbed had to support not only the birds but the fish on which they depended. Recent studies, including doctoral research at the University of Hull, have therefore concentrated on the water conditions needed to sustain native fish, treating the bird and its food supply as a single system.

G. The final concern was longer term. Tracking showed that once independent, young bitterns disperse in their first winter to seek out new wetlands, and that some will settle to breed wherever conditions are suitable. This pointed to an obvious strategy: rather than concentrate the birds in a few vulnerable strongholds, create a spread of new sites for them to colonise. A second EU LIFE project has pursued exactly this, building a network of nineteen sites so that breeding can occur well beyond the original core. The logic is one of insurance as much as expansion, for a dispersed population is far less exposed to chance disasters and to the rising sea levels that threaten low-lying reedbeds. By 2004 the number of booming males had recovered to 55, almost all of the increase occurring on sites managed according to the research. Science had been central to the story, but its lessons took effect only through the patience and sometimes drastic intervention of the landowners and wardens who applied them.

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Bringing Back the Bittern

How research, not luck, reversed the decline of one of Britain’s most secretive birds

A. The bittern is a heron-like wetland bird whose fortunes in Britain have swung dramatically over little more than a century. Breeding birds had vanished entirely by 1886, yet after re-colonisation in the early 1900s the population climbed to a peak of roughly 70 booming, or singing, males in the 1950s. From there it fell sharply, dropping below 20 by the 1990s. By the late 1980s it was obvious that the species was again in trouble, but conservationists faced an awkward problem: they could see the decline without understanding its causes, and almost no reliable information existed on which to base a recovery. Saving the bird would therefore depend less on goodwill than on first learning how it lived.

B. That task was complicated by the bittern itself. Its mottled plumage and retiring habits keep it hidden deep within reedbeds, so the first challenge was simply to develop a dependable way of monitoring a bird that is rarely seen. The solution lay in sound. During the breeding season the male produces a distinctive booming call, and researchers discovered that the acoustic pattern of each bird is effectively unique. By analysing these patterns they could not only establish how many males were present nationally, but also recognise individuals from one year to the next, which in turn allowed local survival rates to be estimated. A bird that resisted direct observation had, in effect, been persuaded to identify itself.

C. With a counting method in place, attention turned to habitat. The earliest insight came not from new fieldwork but from comparison: sites that had lost their booming males were set against those that had kept them. The contrast was revealing. Bitterns had persisted precisely where the natural drying out of reedbeds, a process known as succession, had been deliberately slowed through management. This finding translated directly into action. Broad recommendations on restoring and maintaining reedbeds were drawn up, and EU LIFE funding enabled work at thirteen sites across the core breeding range. Although the project was led by the RSPB, its success depended on many other organisations, an early sign that recovery would be collaborative rather than the work of a single body.

D. General advice, however, was not the same as precise instruction, and the next phase aimed to replace broad guidance with exact prescriptions. By fitting male bitterns with radio tags at the Minsmere and Leighton Moss reserves, researchers could follow where the birds actually fed. A clear preference emerged for the wetter margins of the reedbed, especially the fringes beside larger pools of open water. The average territory covered around twenty hectares, a figure that gave managers a concrete target for how much reedbed a new or restored site would need. The females told a different but equally important story: since they alone incubate the eggs and raise the young, their needs mattered just as much. Of the eighty-seven nests located, most lay in unbroken vegetation well inside the reedbed, yet always where water remained even in the driest weeks of the season.

E. The effect of applying these prescriptions was striking. At Minsmere, where reedbeds were lowered to halt the drying process, the number of booming males climbed steadily from one to ten. Nationally, the population reached its lowest point of just eleven booming males in 1997 and then, for the first time since the 1950s, began to rise. The recovery was not coincidental; it tracked the management work closely, with the clearest gains appearing exactly where the research-based methods had been applied. For a programme that had begun with almost no usable data, the match between effort and outcome was persuasive evidence that the underlying science was sound.

F. Even so, counting adults could not by itself secure the future, and a later phase examined the diet, survival and movements of the chicks. Tiny radio tags fitted to nestlings traced their fate up to fledging and beyond, and the findings were sobering: many chicks never survived, with starvation the most probable cause. The fish they were fed came overwhelmingly from species that penetrate into the reed edge, which shifted the focus of conservation once again. If the chicks were starving, the reedbed had to support not only the birds but the fish on which they depended. Recent studies, including doctoral research at the University of Hull, have therefore concentrated on the water conditions needed to sustain native fish, treating the bird and its food supply as a single system.

G. The final concern was longer term. Tracking showed that once independent, young bitterns disperse in their first winter to seek out new wetlands, and that some will settle to breed wherever conditions are suitable. This pointed to an obvious strategy: rather than concentrate the birds in a few vulnerable strongholds, create a spread of new sites for them to colonise. A second EU LIFE project has pursued exactly this, building a network of nineteen sites so that breeding can occur well beyond the original core. The logic is one of insurance as much as expansion, for a dispersed population is far less exposed to chance disasters and to the rising sea levels that threaten low-lying reedbeds. By 2004 the number of booming males had recovered to 55, almost all of the increase occurring on sites managed according to the research. Science had been central to the story, but its lessons took effect only through the patience and sometimes drastic intervention of the landowners and wardens who applied them.

parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

Conformity

A review of conformity and some of the studies that have been done on it

During your childhood, there will have been some kind of craze which affected all the people in your school. It may have been to do with a particular toy or possibly a must-have item of clothing. It may have been something as simple as a type of pen or as expensive as an electronic games console. Fashion designers, toy manufacturers and anyone else involved in the retail trade love conformity. Set up a craze, especially in the young, and everyone will go for it. In fact, it's an ideal way to sell huge quantities of merchandise. The levels of conformity in consumerism are phenomenal. When you actually stand back and consider how easily we are persuaded that having certain items is the only way we can ensure peace of mind, you see what an important concept conformity is.

Conformity has been described as “yielding to group pressure” (Crutchfield 1962). However, this implies that other people put pressure on us to make us conform, and this is not always the case. A better definition is given by Aronson (1976), who said it was a “change in a person's behaviour or opinions as a result of real or imagined pressure from a person or group of people.” This would make more sense, as often the pressure we feel is imagined. The person or group he refers to would have to be important to us at the time, regardless of their status.

There has been considerable research on conformity. One of the first studies looked at the answers people gave when asked to estimate the number of beans in a bottle (Jennes, 1932). If you have ever entered a 'guess the number' competition, you probably looked at the previous estimates made and based your judgment on what other people had guessed. This is more or less what happened in the Jennes study. First of all, he asked the respondents to give their own estimates, and then he asked them to decide a group estimate. Finally, he asked them alone again and discovered that they had stayed with the group answer.

Probably the most famous study on conformity was undertaken by Asch (1951), when he created a situation where many of his subjects gave answers which were blatantly untrue, rather than contradict the people they were with. He did this by getting his subject to sit round a table with six stooges so that the subject was second to last. He showed them all a large card which had three lines of different lengths drawn on it, labelled A, B and C. He then gave them a card with a single line and asked them to match this in terms of length to one of the lines A, B or C. The stooges gave untrue responses in a number of the trials, and the subjects were left in the situation where they either reported what they saw with their own eyes or conformed to the norm of the group.

When the results were assessed, Asch found that in one out of every three trials where the wrong answer was given, the subject gave the same wrong answer as the stooges. This led to an average level of conformity of 32 per cent. Asch interviewed his subjects after the trials to try to find out why they conformed to an answer which was so obviously wrong. Most of them said that they did not want to cause problems within the group, although they admitted that when they did give wrong answers it made them anxious. [Asch found that when there was just one other person present who did not go along with the majority, no matter how many others there were, it was sufficient to make the subject give the right answer.]

Kelman (1953) described three ways in which people may conform. The first is compliance. In this case, individuals outwardly accept the group’s position, although their personal opinion remains unchanged. This response reduces the risk of tension or unpleasantness within the group and allows relationships to remain harmonised. The findings from the study by Asch show this clearly: participants publicly followed the group’s answer, while privately disagreeing with it. In other situations, people may experience internalisation. Here, individuals come to believe that the group’s judgement is the more valid one. They may rationalise this shift by telling themselves that their own perception was unreliable, such as assuming their eyesight was poor. Sometimes, however, subjects actually seem to change their beliefs because they want to become more like their heroes. If they really want to become part of an in-group, they will start to identify with that group and take on the group's values and beliefs, even if they are different to their own. Kelman calls this identification. It frequently happens with teenagers who want to become more like a peer group in order to be accepted, and suddenly seem to go against all the values and beliefs of their parents.

So why is it that we have to conform? Some people feel confident most of the time, have high self-esteem and do not have to go along with the majority. For most of us, though, how confident we feel varies from day to day, depending on the situation we are in, and this can influence behaviour.
